guest.titre: Head of Applied Research and Analytics
guest.bio_context: Stephen Buschbaum serves as Head of Applied Research and Analytics at TREP, a data modeling and analytics firm specializing in CMBS, commercial real estate, and CLO markets. He conducts in-depth analysis of macroeconomic indicators and their impact on commercial real estate cycles, including detailed examination of inflation data, refinancing trends, and sources and uses of capital in conduit CMBS transactions.

context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to the TREP Wire podcast, the show where commercial real estate meets data and insights. This is our Week in Review for the week ending August 28th, 2026. I'm Haley Keene with TREP, a data modeling and analytics firm for the CMBS, commercial real estate, and CLO markets. I'm with Lonnie Hendry, Chief Product Officer, and Stephen Buschbaum, Head of Applied Research and Analytics. This week, we received another important inflation reading, with both headline and core PCE increasing a reported 0.2% in July. Today, Stephen will unpack why the underlying numbers were somewhat less encouraging than what the headline suggests, as well as what the latest data mean for interest rates and commercial real estate. We'll also discuss the new 50% Canadian tariffs and their potential impact on construction costs, the record sell-off in Dick's Sporting Goods following continued weakness at Footlocker, and Google's unusual purchase of Spirit Airlines' internal corporate data. Then, we'll turn to the $2.2 billion redemption queue facing Invesco's real estate fund and the incentives the firm is offering investors to stay put or contribute additional capital. Finally, in a digging through the data segment, we'll examine sources and uses information from conduit CMBS loans to see how cash-in and cash-out refinancing have changed through the cycle, and what those trends tell us about the amount of equity owners are putting into or taking out of their properties. So, Stephen, what do you make of this PCE report, and how much did rounding affect the way markets interpreted the inflation data? Funny enough, I think rounding had a meaningful effect on the initial reaction, because the reported 0.2% increase looked more reassuring than the underlying number actually was. Just the fact that we're talking about decimal place rounding here to the third place tells you how tenuous and tense this inflation debate is right now, and how much fun they must be having in Jackson Hole this week. So both Headline and Core PCE reported as increasing 0.2% month-over-month in July, but the unrounded Core reading was 0.246, just four thousandths of a percentage point below the threshold that would have rounded the figure up to 0.3%, and likely caused Treasury yields to increase by double the amount that they did on Wednesday morning. After the print, I think the two-year and ten-year increased by anywhere between three and four basis points, and I could just imagine if that print had rounded up to 0.3, I could have easily seen that to double that to, say, six basis points, or even seven basis points sell-off and yield. So that rounding, I think, was a meaningful nuance to this print. Now that may sound like minor technical distinction, but keep in mind, when we're reporting these data, we're almost always reporting that rounded number, and there's a psychological effect there. And so I suspect with that 0.246 number, the debate that will be going on in Jackson Hole will be even more heated. And think back to the last FOMC meeting. Those three members that outright were saying that we need to hike, plus the folks that were kind of on the fence and maybe were eventually going to move into that hike camp if we saw a hotter print. I mean, it's going to be an interesting dynamic here, and there's a lot of Fed speak that I'm sure we'll be actively listening to over the next couple of days. So if we annualize that unrounded monthly increase, core inflation was running at approximately 3%. And I'm sure your figures told a similar story. Headline PCE remained at 3.7, while core PCE held at 3.0. So while the rounded monthly number may have looked encouraging at first glance, the underlying data did not provide a particularly strong signal that inflation is returning to the Federal Reserve's 2% target. pending_qa.q: Why did Dick's Sporting Goods stock decline sharply despite strong core business performance?
pending_qa.r: Dick's Sporting Goods shares fell as much as 28% following weakness at Foot Locker, which Dick's acquired for $2.4 billion in 2025. Foot Locker's comparable sales declined 3.6% last quarter while core Dick's business sales increased nearly 5%. The decline stems from Foot Locker's large mall-based footprint, struggles in the sneaker market where brands compete directly with wholesale partners, and elevated discounting expected to continue through year-end, reinforcing the divide between healthy retailers and chains exposed to enclosed malls.

pending_qa.q: What are the implications of Google purchasing Spirit Airlines' corporate data for enterprise AI training?
pending_qa.r: Google is reportedly paying $10 million for Spirit Airlines' internal corporate data including 10 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, internal documents, spreadsheets and calendars. This real company operating history, stripped of personally identifiable information, provides Google with unprecedented enterprise-scale training data rather than synthetic or AI-generated alternatives. This transaction reflects a new reality where company data has standalone market value regardless of corporate viability, and raises concerns about privacy and security of corporate communications if companies enter bankruptcy.

pending_qa.q: How is Invesco addressing the $2.2 billion redemption queue in its Core Real Estate USA Fund?
pending_qa.r: Invesco is offering a multi-tiered incentive package: existing investors without pending redemptions receive a 20% management fee reduction, new capital contributors of at least $10 million receive a one-year fee waiver, and investors seeking liquidity can participate in a tender offer purchasing shares at 95% of net asset value. Senior management is also committing up to $150 million of their own capital to strengthen alignment. These incentives aim to retain investors, attract new capital to backfill the redemption queue, and provide a visible price for immediate liquidity while rewarding those willing to remain in the fund.

pending_qa.q: How have cash-in and cash-out refinancing patterns shifted across commercial real estate cycles?
pending_qa.r: Analysis of sources and uses data from the 15 largest loans in conduit CMBS transactions—representing 60 to 70% of aggregate principal—shows distinct patterns. In 2021 and 2022, cash-out refinancing dominated with $7.1 billion and $7.6 billion respectively, while cash-in refinancing totaled only $2.1 billion and $2.2 billion. This reflected elevated property values and low interest rates allowing owners to extract accumulated equity. The pattern changed sharply in 2023 as interest rates rose, reversing the dominance of cash-out activity and increasing pressure on borrowers to contribute additional capital or recapitalize properties.
